chapter.title: What a Ref Is
chapter.description: A box React keeps for you, and how it differs from state.

blocks.text: `useRef` returns an object with a single `current` property. React hands you the same object on every render, and changing `current` does not trigger a re-render.

items: **State** is for values the UI displays. Changing it re-renders.
**Ref** is for values the UI does not display. Changing it does not re-render.
State updates are asynchronous; a ref changes the moment you assign to it.
State must be treated as immutable; a ref is meant to be mutated.

blocks.text: If you find yourself wanting the screen to update after changing a ref, you wanted state. A ref change is invisible to React until something else causes a render.

A local variable is recreated on every render, so it forgets. A module-level variable is shared by every instance of the component. A ref is per-instance and survives renders, which is exactly the middle ground.

items: The previous value of a prop, for comparison.
A flag such as 'has this already submitted'.
A DOM node you need to focus, measure or scroll.
An instance of a third-party library.

blocks.text: Pass a ref object to an element's `ref` attribute and React sets `current` to the DOM node after the commit.
`inputRef.current` is `null` during the first render, because the DOM node does not exist yet. Read it inside an effect or an event handler, never in the render body.
Refs are an escape hatch. Use them for things the declarative model genuinely cannot express.

items: Handing a node to a canvas or charting library.

blocks.text: Do not use a ref to set text, classes or styles by hand. React will overwrite your changes on the next render, and the two sources of truth will fight each other.
A ref can also be a function. React calls it with the node when it mounts and with `null` when it unmounts, which is useful when you need to react to the node appearing.

blocks.caption: One ref holding a Map is easier than trying to create refs in a loop.
